We introduce a simple, fundamental task that hinders deep learning models' adaptability to tasks with non-stationary conditions. We call this task Dual Distribution Shift (DDS) and it comprises two tasks with the same visual presentation as well as class distribution, presented one after another during testing, but utilizing different, non-stationary distributions for data generation. Unlike other distribution shift problems, DDS is uniquely designed to simulate real-world learning scenarios in which a model's exposure to data is confined to its training period. We create three DDS datasets from natural sources to assess how well learning generalizes to these new tasks. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that top-performing pre-trained models, utilizing loose assessment metrics, are largely incapable of successfully adapting to DDS. Moreover, our analysis reveals that deep neural networks, utilizing their loose assessment metrics, tend to memorize their initial training data, rendering them incapable of utilizing their acquired knowledge on unseen, new distributions.

Our study focuses on creating a machine-based system to identify human instances of hate speech across multiple modalities. A novel, multi-layered framework is introduced to interpret hate speech through multi-modal, band-specific layers, leveraging both semantic and affective features. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in handling MX-Parl's image and sound inputs for the multi-modal challenge, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and achieving record-breaking accuracy at 77.69. Moreover, the framework's ability to incorporate domain-agnostic layers highlights its capacity to provide understandable multi-modal hate speech identification capabilities.

Neuronal networks, particularly those comprised of Type-I neurons, are widespread in various biological systems. To better understand the behavior of these networks, researchers are exploring numerical and analytical approaches. This paper delves into the effect of different network sizes on the emergence of synchronized behavior, as well as the limitations of existing analytical models. By comparing analytical predictions with numerical simulations, we find that assuming a uniform network distribution may not accurately capture the dynamics of real-world neuronal groups. Our analysis reveals that while analytical models based on average network sizes have some success, they fall short in accurately predicting the emergence of synchronized behavior across all network sizes. Consequently, researchers are developing and examining improved models, such as those that consider a dual scale approach, to better account for the variability of network sizes and their impact on synchronized behavior.

Fixing automated bugs is a complex issue, and most current solutions are hindered by limited training data. To overcome this, we've developed an innovative approach called APCT, leveraging data augmentation through antipodal creation. By generating opposing examples, our method can produce higher-quality correcting patches. We've built upon our prior research on automated program fixing and applied our finding of correcting patch characteristics to apply an analogous principle - opposition - in our algorithm. By training on pairs of opposing correcting patches, our method has been successfully tested on a standard fixing benchmark, revealing performance comparable to state-of-the-art solutions. Our results suggest that understanding correcting patches through counterexamples can yield valuable insights.

A data spectrum has been proposed as a new tool for a type of quantum communication known as quantum information forwarding with untrusted senders. This tool is defined as the maximum rate at which quantum information can be extracted from a specific quantum state ensemble, which is related to the quantum state's entanglement properties. Research has shown that data spectra can characterize the fundamental limits of entanglement creation in quantum states. In this study, the capability boundaries of the data-spectrum-based quantum information forwarding strategy (GIFC) are being investigated, specifically in terms of one-way distillable entanglement. To achieve this, the researchers derived upper and lower limits for one-way distillable entanglement, along with corresponding protocols for its computation. Additionally, the findings demonstrate that one-way distillable entanglement serves as a reliable measure of quantum information. When compared to another distillation measure, it was found that one-way distillable entanglement provides a broader range of applicability, especially when considering the GIFC strategy.

The development of 3-dimensional flow examination has enabled researchers to conduct more thorough analyses of flow data in multiple directions. By studying the symmetric 2-nucleon correlation functions in heavy-ion collisions, researchers can investigate the impact of 3-dimensional data on various parameters such as nuclear radii and Coulomb barrier heights. By comparing these parameters with 1-dimensional analyses, researchers can determine the additional information 3-dimensional data provides. Additionally, researchers used 3-dimensional flow examination to investigate the stiffening of the Equation-of-State in 124 MeV Au+Au collisions, revealing significant discrepancies between 1-dimensional and 3-dimensional analyses. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating 3-dimensional data in flow analyses to uncover new insights into Equations-of-State, particularly in the range of 30-80 MeV.

Due to the severe health risks and high costs associated with conventional COVID-19 testing methods, alternative, high-throughput testing methods are being developed. This study explores whether enhanced image acoustics testing can accurately detect early-stage COVID-19 patients, and if so, what neural network models can be used to achieve this goal while safeguarding patient privacy through adversarial training techniques. Our research utilized a unique dataset consisting of CT images, audio recordings, and relevant patient information from a hospital in China. Experiments were performed to evaluate different adversarial training strategies in boosting the ability of neural networks to recognize COVID-19 patients, and the results showed that image-based early detection rates could reach up to 90% through adversarial training, surpassing non-trained models significantly. Our study also shed light on the effectiveness of various adversial training techniques and their impact on training efficiency and accuracy.

The growing reliance on wireless communication systems necessitates that these networks support complex tasks such as navigation and object recognition by intelligent devices. However, performing such tasks requires substantial wireless transmission bandwidth, which poses significant challenges. To address this issue, this paper proposes an innovative wireless transmission system designed to convey graph data efficiently. Our proposed decentralized reasoning system utilizes Graph Neural Networks to process graph data and output predicted results, demonstrating that it can perform comparable tasks with less data transmission than current systems. Our results show that the decentralized reasoning system achieves 96.67% classification accuracy with 50% reduced graph data transmission in object recognition tasks, outperforming existing solutions.

Brazilian municipalities are divided into clusters by the Ministry of Security, but there have been concerns over its transparency and the accuracy of the data used for other government purposes, including homicide rates. Our analysis of homicide rates over 12 years revealed that the Ministry established three distinct clustering systems using different levels of detail and statistical significance. Two datasets analyzed yielded local complete and incomplete groupings, and removing insignificant areas resulted in a separate clustering system. Our study's findings suggest that the systems differ in their distribution of cluster sizes and the proportion of small clusters.

We examine the performance of probabilistic learning methods, including Bayesian techniques, under challenging conditions where data contains a significant proportion of mislabelled or malicious data. These methods are generally more resilient than their deterministic counterparts in such scenarios. However, they may struggle when data has been manipulated intentionally, as is the case with Advanced Adversarial Examples (AAAs). While conventional optimization algorithms can be made adaptive to AAAs by increasing their iteration counts, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) may require a substantial number of iterations, which could be impractically high. To address this issue, we investigate a variant of SGD known as stochastic gradient ascent with acceleration (SGAA), which demonstrates a notable ability to reduce the required iterations while maintaining robust performance against both random noise and AAA data.

A newly developed Kikuchi camera, BabyIAXO, has been designed for the Sun's core analysis, boasting 10 iron-57 source lines sensitivity within the 18.5-22.5 keV range. Utilizing Kondo effect line broadening, this technology enables the measurement of the Sun's center temperature distribution with remarkable precision, achieving an accuracy of approximately 1.5 keV. In addition to temperature distribution, BabyIAXO can also make precise estimates of the magnetic field strength within the Sun's core, achieving an accuracy of approximately 10 Gauss. Through comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations, the capabilities of BabyIAXO were thoroughly examined, demonstrating its ability to accurately measure the solar core temperature with an accuracy of around 10 keV and provide detailed insights into the sun's core transport properties, specifically the normalized muon Lande g-factor (g_mu). Furthermore, the technology has significant implications for understanding the sun's core convection processes, offering a detailed understanding of its transport properties.

We introduce a new class of systems with unique properties that differ from traditional self-exciting systems like the Lintner model. These systems, in contrast, consistently predict lower growth rates, estimate growth more accurately in the long term, and show that short-term estimates tend to be optimistically biased. To be qualified as self-exciting, a theoretical model must meet two criteria: demonstrating the approach to the long-term estimate as time goes to infinity and showing that increasing time since the last adjustment leads to a decrease in estimated growth rate. We develop a theoretical model to illustrate a scenario that fails these self-exciting criteria.

This article introduces DexGraspNet, a universal object grasp dataset designed to enhance robotic grasping skills. Unlike existing datasets limited by specific domain data, DexGraspNet can be applied across various regions of space. We employ a high-throughput deep learning-based simulation to efficiently generate diverse four-finger gripper grasp samples. By applying filtering criteria, we narrow down these samples to ensure high success rates with a universal two-finger gripper. We compile DexGraspNet-15K using simulation and further expand it to DexGraspNet-68K using real-world data with a commercial robot. We propose a new evaluation metric that assesses both grasp feasibility and quality. Our approach also utilizes a physics-based metric to differentiate between training and testing datasets, preventing data contamination. Through comprehensive experiments with popular grasp prediction models, we demonstrate DexGraspNet-68K's effectiveness in improving manipulation performance over previous datasets.

This research presents an innovative free-breathing motion adjusted four-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo MRI sequence. The proposed sequence is designed to study motion artifacts in MRI, specifically in the context of respiratory motion in the thorax and abdominal areas. A novel approach was developed to reduce the impact of moving organs during data collection. The proposed sequence is unique in that it is not limited to a specific imaging location and can be applied to the entire body. A series of studies were conducted to compare image quality and data consistency between the proposed sequence and a conventional navigator-gated sequence. The proposed sequence showed significant improvements in data consistency and overall scan time. A substantial reduction in the evaluation time and image analysis time was observed when using the proposed sequence. A wide range of applications was identified for the proposed sequence, including the assessment of free-breathing MRI, whole abdomen imaging, and hepatocellular carcinoma evaluation. These findings suggest that the proposed sequence is a valuable addition to the MRI toolset, particularly in the abdominal and thoracic regions.

This paper presents InDistill, a novel knowledge distillation technique, to diminish the computational requirements of deep learning models for real-time applications on embedded platforms. Traditional model reduction methods often result in loss of critical data between network layers, leading to significant performance degradation. InDistill leverages teacher-student distillation to simplify the teacher model by combining layer outputs, maintaining data flow and improving reduction efficiency. We demonstrate InDistill on deep SqueezeNet networks, achieving a 2.7x smaller and 1.55 faster deployment on edge embedded systems, while surpassing current state-of-the-art distillation methods.

Our main objective is to establish a method for classifying submersion functions based on the topological equivalence of their level set foliations. In doing so, we propose a novel approach that leverages classification criteria for linear-like foliations established in our earlier research. Specifically, we derive conditions under which this method effectively categorizes submersion functions classified as linear-like. Furthermore, we introduce and analyze a submersion function that defies our initial results under certain conditions but aligns with them in a particular scenario.

In desert landscapes, water is the deciding factor for plant growth, and their proximity to water sources is crucial for their survival. Plants in these environments have the ability to tap into underground water through root systems, and their success is influenced by their ability to access this water. Research has shown that root systems can extend beyond the area above ground, and this non-local characteristic can have significant implications for plant dynamics. A mathematical model was developed to simulate plant behavior in desert landscapes, and it revealed that non-local root systems can create patterns of plant clustering, contrary to plant distribution when plants' root systems are confined to the area above ground. These findings have the potential to improve our understanding of plant behavior in desert ecosystems, and their implications are far-reaching.

The CountSketch data structure is known for efficiently performing moment estimation and providing resistance against input manipulation to achieve approximate statistical query accuracy to order. However, its ability to resist adaptive inputs that have partial access to it remains unresolved in the literature. In this research, we investigate how CountSketch handles adaptive inputs, specifically those that can access up to a fraction of it, to approach a moment estimation lower bound. To this end, we present a CountSketch that can successfully estimate the first and second moments of an input, even when the input has access to a fraction of it, and for any moment of order $p \geq 2$. This data structure also outperforms traditional CountSketch when dealing with adaptive inputs, and in cases where CountSketch equals traditional CountSketch, its size is within a constant factor. Furthermore, our results are supported by an adversarial input, which can access a fraction of the moment, and for any other distribution, our results are within a constant factor.

The ipie package, developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo calculations, is now publicly available on Python repositories, allowing users to easily install it via pip or conda. This package offers a flexible and efficient platform for performing AFMC simulations, incorporating a range of advanced features such as a parallelized variational Monte Carlo engine, a system for handling symmetry, and a system for calculating correlation lengths and spectral functions. Key innovations include a parallelized implementation that takes advantage of complex algorithms, a system for modeling spin-orbit coupling and external magnetic fields, and a system for optimizing Monte Carlo sampling through open and closed MC updates. Additionally, ipie supports both CPU and GPU hardware acceleration, enabling efficient utilization of custom GPU implementations through a custom device module. This paper describes ipie's architecture and provides case studies highlighting its performance advantages over other auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo software packages using systems such as Kr and Mo.

This research explores how quantum techniques can transform the core principles of game theory through the application of multi-player games in quantum systems.  By integrating frequency trading within this framework, we demonstrate the potential for quantum strategies to fundamentally alter market dynamics in existing systems.  Moreover, utilizing real-frequency trading data as classical strategies in the n-LISERD game, we achieve a significant improvement in market stability and efficiency through faster settlement times and higher overall volume.  Our game's equilibrium also exhibits greater resilience to market shocks, showcasing a promising path for quantum-enhanced financial markets in the future.

This study examines how the presence of middlemen affects the optimal behavior of rational agents, using a standard signaling framework where the impact of middlemen is measured by the loss of potential income compared to an ideal scenario with no information leakage. Our analysis shows that middlemen's loss of information can be minimized or completely avoided under specific conditions, provided that certain requirements are met.

To effectively generate reconstrutive summaries, summarization models need to decide which words within the generate text should correspond to which input words. Currently, most planning-based approaches rely on the entire input sentence as a prompt for the model at each prediction step. In this research, we investigate the potential of using acquired entity prompts, where the model collects and learns to use specific entity names extracted from summaries generated so far. A new method called AEPL is proposed, where a set of acquired entity prompts is used alongside the input sentence for the GPT-3 model to generate outputs at each prediction step. Notably, AEPL shows significant improvements in using shorter prompts compared to existing planning-based approaches, achieving comparable performance while requiring fewer parameters and tokens. Additionally, our method can be combined with other existing techniques to yield comparable results to more complex models.

This study focuses on a multivariate function y defined over an open subset D in n-dimensional space, whose partial derivatives with respect to n-1 variables are continuous and defined over the same space. We examine the logical equivalence between the differentiability of these partial derivatives and the differentiability of y, particularly in cases where one variable is held fixed and another varies. 

When considering an arbitrary point within D and fixing all but two variables, we obtain a binary function related to y. By analyzing this relationship, we aim to establish a connection between the differentiability of the partial derivatives of y and the differentiability of y itself. Notably, our investigation involves exploring how fixing certain variables, and varying two others, relates to overall differentiability.

However, this connection is particularly challenging when one of the fixed variables corresponds to a boundary point of D in its corresponding partial derivative. By leveraging properties of neighborhoods and open sets, we demonstrate a non-trivial scenario where partial derivatives' differentiability does not necessarily translate to the differentiability of y. Furthermore, this boundary situation is particularly pertinent in cases where one variable represents time within a given domain.

Ultimately, our work contributes to understanding the intricate relationships between multivariate functions and their partial derivatives in diverse mathematical settings.

Despite ongoing research on vocal entrainment, a universally accepted definition is still lacking. In this paper, a clear operationalization of vocal entrainment within dyadic dialogues is presented as subtle adjustments in production timing. Building upon existing work on automatic vocal entrainment detection, a new complex model is proposed that considers both local and contextual factors. Notably, entrainment tendencies vary significantly depending on the dialogue context. Through leave-one-out cross-validation experiments, a computational model using support vector regression achieved improved performance compared to a baseline with an adjusted average absolute error of 0.155 seconds. These results confirm the existence of vocal entrainment and its dependence on dialogue context, thereby supporting theories on vocal entrainment's underlying mechanisms.

This study explores the concept of quantum regulation within the framework of the unitary sphere, introducing a novel structure called the unitary sphere with a line, denoted as the unitary sphere-line or UΛS1, comprising a sphere of radius one and an internal segment of radius two. Our research reveals that UΛS1 is a comprehensive and fundamental structure, encompassing numerous other spherical structures as distinct instances. We also develop a category of continuous, one-parameter groups of unitary operators, providing a robust framework to investigate the relationships between UΛS1 and similar structures, thereby offering valuable insights into the construction of regular and stable physical theories. By analyzing uLS1's behavior in comparison to λS1 under different conditions, this research contributes to the theoretical understanding of physical processes and the development of reliable models.

We've derived analytical expressions for two types of quasiparticle disturbances within fractional quantum Hall states, and our results are essentially exact, with the sole significant approximation being the presence of an external magnetic field. We employed a computational approach called a symplectic transform to calculate quasiparticle wave functions in this strong magnetic environment. This approach relies on the expansion of wave functions using an orthogonal polynomial basis, which we determined by applying the three-step method: initially, we mapped an angular momentum basis onto a symplectic basis, then solved for the transformation matrix using a quasi-classical approximation, and finally, utilized this matrix to obtain expressions for physical properties. These expressions are evaluated as power series in the inverse magnetic field strength, which we computed for up to seven terms for a Laughlin state and four terms for both a Pfian and an anti-Laughlin state.

In order to approximate the solution of a semicoercive Stokes variational inequality that models glacier dynamics, various techniques have been applied to adapt established methods for handling oblique derivative boundary conditions to derive limited post hoc error estimates for finite element approximations.

We have analyzed data from the VLT/AMBER instrument, observing a starbursting disk galaxy (SDS1005+0114) at a redshift of 2.11, which exhibits robust 12CO emission, which we used to pinpoint a star-forming region. The data from AMBER, which covered a range of stellar masses, showed that the majority of CO emission originates from a compact starburst region, which we resolved spatially for the first time. This region is characterized by extensive gas and dust, which we used to study the impact of massive star formation on its surroundings. The CO velocity field revealed a complex structure, which we attributed to the effects of massive star formation, including galactic winds and the impact of massive star formation on the galaxy's rotation. The data also showed that the outer regions of the galaxy exhibit a significant degree of turbulence, which we attributed to the effects of massive star formation and the formation of massive stars.

The triangular potential is introduced in a multiphase transport model to investigate its impact on the triangular flow $v_3$. Introducing a specific source anisotropy at the beginning of the simulation, we observed a significant increase in $v_3$ that aligns well with experimental data from Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at a specific midrapidity range. Notably, the $v_3$ values from our simulation exceed those based on average $v_3$ measurements, that is, $v_3$ values derived from a fit to $v_3$ and $p_T$-weighted averages. This discrepancy, however, resolves when considering $v_3$ measurements at midrapidity and within a specific $|y|$ range, that is, $y$ values between -0.5 and -0.5. Furthermore, we observed that the $v_3$ values are largely unaffected by changes in initial conditions and a specific anisotropic term coefficient, that is, $V_3^0$, and are instead primarily determined by the hydrodynamic evolution.

This research introduces the concept of SimSura, a novel robotic system capable of generating three-dimensional structures on demand. By utilizing a single 6-DoF robotic arm, paired with an end-effector consisting of an electric motor, a camera, and an infrared sensor, SimSura can simultaneously plan, monitor, and execute the creation of structures. A key innovation of SimSura is the integration of an active gripper, which allows for adaptive construction of beams while accounting for uncertainty in their positioning. Moreover, SimSura's architecture is designed to facilitate creation of beams in any 3D space, and its image processing capabilities allow for real-time uncertainty assessment and feedback. Ultimately, SimSura's capabilities are showcased through experimental results demonstrating its potential for accurate simultaneous structure creation and uncertainty reduction.

The latest breakthrough in semantic segmentation has shown that pre-training models using depth assessment tasks improves performance beyond traditional image classification. This improvement has been attributed to the rich spatial information gained from monocular depth estimation. However, we argue that depth assessment models also provide valuable semantic information, particularly when we utilize multi-scale depth loss functions. Moreover, we found that a simple depth assessment task combining scale reconstruction and semantic segmentation loss can effectively replace the complex monocular depth estimation loss when fine-tuning. Surprisingly, we discovered that a depth assessment model can even substitute the semantic loss within a training pipeline, leading to better results. Specifically, we found that a training method using monocular depth estimation instead of a dedicated semantic loss can outperform the current state-of-the-art semantic segmentation techniques. The experiments demonstrate that a monotonic depth loss trend can be observed when we incorporate depth assessment in both pre-training and fine-tuning. The exceptional results we found when using a depth assessment model in the semantic segmentation task suggest that spatial and semantic signals obtained from depth estimation are more valuable than those obtained from image classification.

This study aims to determine the enhanced Bohr radius within the context of the class $S^*_H$ of the form factor $h reel \theta/r$ where $|h(real \theta/r)| \leq r$, specifically focusing on harmonic mappings $f$ from the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ to itself that satisfy $f(0)=0$, with $f$ being orientation-preserving. We find that the enhanced Bohr radius $R_B^+$ for this class is the positive real root of the equation $r^3-r^2+1/4=0$, with the corresponding Bohr radius being the root of $r^2+r+1/4=0$. Moreover, we establish sharpness for both of these values.

This study introduces an efficient approach for computing confidence intervals for Kendall's tau by resolving a long-standing limitation associated with its standard estimator. A significant challenge arises from the high variance of the typical confidence interval method, caused by Kendall's tau being bounded, resulting in many nominal 95% intervals actually having a 70-80% coverage probability. To overcome this problem, a new normalizing estimator is proposed, leveraging a well-known limiting distribution to create more accurate confidence intervals. Notably, these new intervals demonstrate substantially reduced variance compared to their traditional counterparts, as validated through extensive simulations. Furthermore, computational experiments involving large datasets show the considerable practical advantage of the novel normalizing estimator.

In the realm of IoT, particularly within smart cities, autonomous vehicles pose particular challenges. To safeguard personal data in vehicular networks, a proposed solution involves implementing a privacy-focused collaborative framework. This approach employs information theory's min-entropy as a metric for information secrecy. A secrecy-preserving edge cloud, which monitors each participant's data, identifies and verifies their credibility. Upon validation, the participant's weights are incorporated into a global model constructed using a federated learning methodology. This novel framework has been rigorously evaluated through simulations to demonstrate the efficacy of both the collaborative structure and the proposed data and communication protocols.

A novel approach to visualizing point clouds is introduced through the significance surface framework, where a novel statistical measure indicates the concentration of points in a given area. By applying this technique to datasets comprising synthetic and real data points, the approach yields multiple valuable visual insights.

The onset of the Allee effect is a pressing concern in ecological research, particularly in the development of population dynamical models. Investigating its impact on the long-term behavior of species is a crucial area of investigation. This study delves into the Allee effect's influence on the Holling-Tanner predator-prey model, exploring how it affects both prey and predator populations. By incorporating an Allee effect driven by competition into the prey population, researchers modified the traditional Holling-Tanner model to create a new system. This modification led to the creation of four distinct systems to examine. Three of these systems exhibit stable populations, consisting of stable nodes, stable limit cycles, and coexisting stable populations, respectively. Notably, one of these models possesses an unstable saddle-man, serving as a separatrix, thereby determining whether populations thrive or face extinction. This research provides significant insights into the Allee effect's influence on predator-prey systems, particularly those incorporating logistic and Beverton-Holt functions governing the predator's response to prey availability.

Our previous research introduced the 'aspect pivot' approach for creating finite convergence simplex algorithms for linear optimization problems. These algorithms' performance is evaluated through several criteria: (a) avoiding degeneracy; (b) bounding the distance of successive iterates; (c) bounding the distance of successive iterates by a linearly decreasing function of the objective function value improvement; and (d) bounding the distance of successive iterates relative to the objective function value improvement in a linear manner. This research establishes that the non-degenerate algorithm developed in the first paper satisfies criterion (c). Building upon this, a modified 'aspect pivot' approach has been proposed to address criteria (b) and (c) simultaneously, specifically for problems with a fixed number of variables and constraints.

We establish that for a graded ring R and N > 1, the NK_1 collective group for the graded nil radical of R is vanishing. This is achieved by demonstrating that the same property holds for the graded nil ideal of R when it is considered as an ungraded R-module. This result aligns with prior research by Rowen and the author, who proved a similar vanishing property for the NK_1 collective group of the graded nil ideal under specific conditions.

Using the ALICE generator, we examined how including in-shell and excluded off-shell states impacts extraction of the $x_t$ weight for $tt$ production at LHCb. Our analysis revealed that when off-shell $tt$ contributions are removed from $\mathcal{P}_{37}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{46}$ distributions, their average values significantly decrease to $x_t = 1.38 \pm 0.13$ and $x_t = 1.36 \pm 0.13$, compared to their original estimates. Notably, when these contributions are also removed from $\mathcal{P}_{37}$ and $\mathcal{P}_{46}$ distributions with an additional filter for isolated leptons, we found $x_t = 1.49 \pm 0.14$ and $x_t = 1.47 \pm 0.13$, respectively. Our results demonstrate that ignoring off-shell $tt$ states results in a bias of over 10% in the estimated $x_t$ weight.

In practical settings, anti-spoofing models are frequently compromised by deliberate spoofing techniques aimed at fooling them. Recent research has introduced global face spoofing measures that employ masks to challenge live/replay detection models more effectively than localized spoofing methods. However, these global measures have a relatively high production cost. In contrast, zero-shot global face spoofing measures require minimal computation and do not necessitate any annotation, making them even more efficient than their localized counterparts. Two novel zero-shot global face spoofing measures are presented in this paper, the first simply involves replicating the facial region from a given fraudulent image, while the second involves generating masks by combining and modifying multiple facial features from diverse images to create unpredictable global spoofing measures. These proposed global spoofing measures are evaluated on prominent anti-spoofing evaluation platforms, including LDES, CASIA, and XES2, utilizing cutting-edge models like ResNet and ViT. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed global spoofing measures over the previously effective localized spoofing measures, with a relatively low computational cost.

The ProC is a modular, plug-and-play software framework for developing AI-driven control systems. It facilitates a step-by-step, model-free approach to solving complex control tasks. The system is based on Deep Q-Network (DQN) and Double DQN algorithms, which can be combined with various soft-computing methods to address different task requirements. The system is designed to be highly customizable, allowing for the integration of different perception algorithms and adaptable algorithm components. It also supports efficient training through parallel processing on GPU-PC combinations and allows for deployment on graphics cards of different architectures.

A novel variant of time-based parent selection is introduced within the realm of Parallel Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (PMOEA). This innovative selection scheme, termed frequency-centered, is designed to minimize the influence of evaluation time bias that can arise from the sequential ordering of evaluations in parallel computing environments. To illustrate the efficacy of the proposed parent selection, a modified version of a widely-used PMOE/A, fast Pareto Archive Evolutionary Algorithm (Pareto/ago/PA), is presented. This variant, Pareto/PA-FS, was subjected to thorough empirical evaluation across various benchmark functions and real-world problems, and demonstrated superior performance across the board, including achieving better solutions with significantly reduced computational effort.

The detection of an exoplanet's microlensing event, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, was announced, featuring an estimated mass of 5.3 MJupiter. This discovery represents a crucial component in the current understanding of exoplanetary systems, particularly those resembling Jupiter analogs. Leveraging data from the Keck Adaptive Lensing project, an independent analysis of an ALE image captured in 2019 yielded a refined orbital path for OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, ultimately enabling its classification as a free-floating planet. Subsequent research using ALE images from 2019 and 2021 further solidified its status as a non-gravitationally bound celestial body. This discovery marks a notable addition to the growing population of confirmed sub-Jupiter mass planets identified through microlensing, with a key distinction being its substantial distance from its host star and minimal surface temperature. As a result, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb stands out as a promising target for a comprehensive characterization of its atmospheric properties, utilizing a combination of JWST and ALE technology in the near future.

A recent expansion developed by Pollock and Andriyenko provides a precise mathematical framework for describing time-evolving quantum states within a finite-dimensional space. Key features of this expansion, which is unique to the Lindblad equation, are its ability to accurately represent regular functions over the entire real number axis at a high rate. Key parameters of its performance, specifically convergence rate and approximation error, can be easily identified. The expansion is unique in providing these features while maintaining the physical constraints of the Lindblad equation. The study demonstrates this power with two applications, including approximating quantum state oscillations triggered by sinusoidal perturbations, and deriving efficient master equations for time-evolving Lindblad generators through a reparametrization of time.

Neutron depolarization measurements are used to study spin disorder in alloys,
which can be affected by magnetic impurities. Depolarization can arise from both
non-magnetic multiple scattering and the effects of spin-dependent phenomena.
However, when spin immobilization leads to multiple spin-dependent scattering,
it results in significant depolarization. By examining how this depolarization
correlates with Curie temperatures in a series of CePd$_{1-y}$Rh$_y$ alloys,
researchers can determine whether spin immobilization contributes to this
behavior. They find that neutron depolarization tracks the phase diagram's range
from a pure Ce_pd host to a pure Rh host, indicating that alloys near the
curie temperature exhibit substantial influences from spin immobilization on
f-electron behavior.

A star-forming complex known as G176.51+00.20, located in the Milky Way, is home to a massive star-forming region surrounded by high-velocity gas streams. This research explores the origins of these streams and their connection to high-speed outflows generated by massive star formation using 12CO, 13CO, and H I observations. Our findings reveal that the gas streams originate from a merger of two distinct structures, likely resulting from the formation of G176.51+00.20. Notably, the study discovered that the gas streams exhibit properties indicative of a high-velocity cloud colliding with the star-forming complex. Furthermore, the research identified high-speed outflows generated by massive star formation, characterized by velocities exceeding 30 km/s and extending up to 4.5 pc. These outflows are believed to be driven by the formation of massive stars and have the potential to impact their surroundings.

All finite words sharing the same relative frequencies of letters are referred to as having the same $\beta$-weight. We have established that every $\beta$-weight equivalence class contains a special kind of word called a 'lexicographically maximal word with a gap', and this study demonstrates that taking the union of two such special words always results in another lexicographically maximal word with a gap, which implies that they form a structured system under the direct product operation. This finding suggests that this subsemigroup is isomorphic to a transformation semigroup consisting of positive integer sequences, which we have started to understand in terms of its underlying structure. Our understanding of this semigroup is based on an initial step, as it is part of a larger, more complex area that remains open to exploration.

Measuring CP violation in neutral meson mixings is a crucial aspect of particle physics, and this work focuses on determining the CP-violating phase phi_s in Bs to J/psi pi plus J/psi pi minus transitions. Using data from 7/3 fb^-1 of LHCb's pp collisions at 1.45 TeV, researchers measured phi_s with two methods: employing B^0_s tags and jet-assisted tagging. The phi_s values were found to be 0.04 ± 0.12 + 0.06 - 0.07 statistical and systematics error, respectively. After combining these measurements, phi_s was found to be 0.03 ± 0.07. Furthermore, phi_s was observed to be consistent with the Standard Model prediction of nearly zero, and inconsistent with a large CP-violating signal at greater than 5.9 standard deviations from zero.

Deep neural networks excel at solving specific tasks but are limited to specific data environments. When faced with different data types, their performance typically declines. This study compares various domain adaptation techniques applied to deep neural networks, including feature mapping, representation learning, and risk control, using a practical example. The research utilized a pre-trained network to identify bird species within nest images but encountered a migration scenario, as the trained dataset included nest images, while the testing dataset consisted of direct bird images. The assessment revealed that the risk control technique known as CORA outperformed other adaptation techniques in this context, although enforcing higher model confidence yielded subpar results, and the evaluation metrics utilized were deemed unsuitable for handling domain migration challenges.

In this context, the points $\lambda$ and $\\mu$ are excluded to ensure the arc can extend to infinity. The points on the curve can be classified into generic points and special points, with specific conditions for each. The curve can be divided into sets based on these classifications. This research paper explores the concept of demonstrating without words, a method that combines art and mathematics to convey understanding through visual demonstrations rather than written explanations. The paper demonstrates this idea using triangles within a grid by presenting several theorems with accompanying visual demonstrations, including an elegant proof of Pythagoras' theorem. Additionally, the study delves into the properties of a triangle inscribed in a grid by examining key points such as the centroid, incenter, orthocenter, circumcenter, and the Euler line, all presented through visual demonstrations.

This study introduces the Parameterized Graph Interpreter (PGI), a novel search-based approach to design graph neural networks (GNNs) that incorporates pre-existing gnn modules as its base units. By utilizing PGI, we can effectively identify the most suitable search architecture and parameterize it with fixed values, thus avoiding the need for a labor-intensive end-to-end search without prior weight initializations. Our research shows that PGIs produce competitive results and outperforms pre-trained weight initializations in both a straightforward and complex task, while also demonstrating its ability to find a search architecture that matches the performance of the top-ranking Evolving Graph Neural Networks (E-GNN) algorithm, a state-of-the-art search method, but at a significantly reduced computational cost and time.

The Coma cluster's member galaxy, RXCJ0232.2-4420, exhibits unusual characteristics when compared to standard spiral galaxies. Discovered by the ROSAT X-ray satellite, the galaxy is surrounded by a massive X-ray emitting halo. We have analyzed archival data from various instruments to study the galaxy, including HST observations at visible and infrared wavelengths, and XMM-Newton and Chandra data at X-ray wavelengths. The galaxy appears to be isolated within the cluster, with its X-ray emission likely caused by the hot interstellar medium within it. The galaxy is located at the center of a dense star cluster, with significant globular cluster content. The galaxy's X-ray halo has been further investigated using Chandra data. The data suggests that the galaxy lies at the center of the X-ray emission, with the X-ray halo likely caused by the hot interstellar medium within it. The galaxy's X-ray luminosity is consistent with that of other systems that have experienced recent gas stripping events. By comparing the galaxy's stellar mass to that of other galaxies with similar properties, we can estimate the galaxy's distance to be at $z=0.0324\pm0.0004$.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Module (LMM), a novel type of recurrent neural network, has emerged as a leading contender in processing time-series data, including forecasting and outlier detection tasks. Its simplified design and high performance make it particularly appealing for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Nonetheless, the most efficient existing methods for training LMM still face a significant bottleneck, the CPU-based solver for the Schwinger-Keldysh (SK) integral, which is essential for calculating the output. To overcome this limitation, we successfully parallelized the CPU solver, thereby reducing training times by up to 80 times. Our approach leverages the LMM's inherent spatial and temporal parallelism to enable fast training. Additionally, we conducted a thorough investigation into the memory module's design space and the impact of memory operations on training, shedding light on the complexities of optimizing LMM.

This review outlines the current knowledge of experimentally detected neutral particles, with a primary focus on previously invisible particles that have been identified through direct and high-energy beam experiments. The discussion then shifts to speculative theories of new neutral particles. The naturally occurring particles, with their known masses and interaction strengths, are examined as a baseline for understanding hidden sectors. The standard model of weakly-interacting particles is then described as a bridge to hidden sectors of theories beyond the standard model. The direct search for invisible particles has a long history, beginning with Eötvös's search for dark matter. The discussion on beam experiments starts by examining the null results of searches for low-energy forces between macroscopic objects. The review then delves into high-energy beam experiments, highlighting searches for inelastic particle collisions that involve newly discovered particles. The discussion on production mechanisms highlights the role of gauge boson mixing in particle creation. The review concludes by examining the constraints on particle couplings, emphasizing the importance of both weak and gravitational interactions in particle search experiments.

Linguistic data consists of multiple labels that convey the same tag for a given record, which poses a significant challenge in the field of multi-view clustering where each record is assigned a categorical label from various experts. To effectively address this issue, we introduce a novel game-based model, which incorporates a dynamic strategy in a modified Braess' paradox scenario involving two types of players - migrating and non-migrating. Our goal is to achieve a consensus on labels by maximizing the system's overall utility, which we define as the sum of the log probabilities of players' chosen strategies. By comparing our model to the original Braess' paradox and demonstrating the existence of a Nash equilibrium in the modified game, we ensure the convergence of our labeling system towards a consistent labeling matrix. Moreover, we illustrate the trade-off between system utility and record coverage in labeling, which helps to clarify the link between label consistency and system utility. Ultimately, our computational results show that a small group of migrating players can drive the system towards a consensus on labels.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly used to solve partial differential equations. Their performance largely depends on choosing appropriate optimization parameters. This study examines how incorporating momentum into PINNs affects their optimization. By combining the insights from neural tangent kernel theory and PINN research, we find that adding momentum reduces the bias toward learning simple functions early on, thereby allowing for a more balanced initial focus on complex functions. This discovery holds true for a range of problems under a few practical assumptions. By building upon existing research that has shown the benefits of momentum, our results provide further evidence that utilizing momentum within PINNs can be advantageous. A thorough discussion of how early optimization behavior impacts PINN's overall accuracy is also included in our findings.

We investigate a system of interconnected wave equations where the Kelvin-Voigt damping is applied in a limited area. We're proving the system leads to exponential stability under the condition that all waves have even numbers when counted, including those reflected. A comparable approach can be used for the case where Kelvin-Voigt damping is applied in a limited area within the context of connected wave equations overall stability under the GKS condition. A connectedness requirement is not needed for achieving local exponential stability in the context of interconnected wave operators on a line domain.

Reinforcement learning agents, modeled using Markov Decision Processes, are successful but often lack transparency, making it challenging for people to understand their learning process. To address this issue, we're working on developing an explanation generation system that can provide clear insights into the decision-making process of models based on Markov Decision Processes with options. To achieve this, we've developed a method for dynamically learning high-level behaviors from low-level interactions between agents and environments. To ensure the learned behaviors are efficient and effective, our system uses a multi-objective learning approach. To facilitate better learning, our system decomposes behaviors into smaller, more manageable sub-behaviors, and represents them using logical rules, which can be easily learned. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we've conducted several experiments based on established benchmarks and tested our system's ability to generate understandable explanations based on logical rules compared to model-free systems, which can't produce such explanations.

A long-standing puzzle in quantum mechanics involves the Asymmetric Quantum Rotation effect first discovered in 1979, which reveals that a spin-1/2 system undergoes different rotation paths clockwise and counter-clockwise when viewed from above, despite having the same underlying Hamiltonian.  Recent research has tackled this mystery through the development of a frame-dependent geometric phase theory and different approaches to quantum compression.  Our work sheds new light on the rotation-path inequality using a concept of compressibility based on path length.  Our results establish that a rotation path's compressibility depends on its direction of circulation and is directly linked to its geometric phase.

We examine a function $f$ that maps from the $n$-dimensional space to the real numbers by expressing it as the sum of shifted versions of a base function $g$, denoted as $f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^N g(t_i + x)$ for all possible $x$ in the $n$-dimensional space, where the base function $g$ is even and has a specific form of decay at infinity. Our goal is to find a function $u$ that minimizes the function $J(u) = \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} I(u,f)$, where the function $I(u,f)$ is defined as the integral of the function $f(u)^2$ over the domain, and to identify conditions under which this function $u$ uniquely minimizes the function $J(u)$. Our study reveals that such a function $u$ exists and is unique under the given conditions on $g$, and we further study the properties of this function $u$ in specific cases where $g$ has a specific form of decay.

The study of particle dark matter interactions with $^6$Li, specifically those involving a spin-dependent, mediators-based force, is being explored. In this investigation, the strengths of DM-nucleus interactions are being quantified by examining both direct detection experiments, as performed by CRESST, and gamma-ray spectroscopy data. By combining these findings, bounds on certain parameters, such as the DM-nucleus scattering cross-section, are being established for different dark matter masses. As a result, significant restrictions are being placed on this type of DM-nucleus interaction.

Blind Image Restoration (BIR) focuses on restoring a degraded image based solely on its single observation when the imaging process's parameters are unknown. A previous approach, Key Image Restoration, assumed pixel values followed a log-normal distribution and identified the best mapping from a key image to the original by optimizing loss function performance, even without knowing the imaging parameters. However, assuming pixel values are log-normally distributed is not always accurate, and even if they were, finding the optimal key image becomes computationally impractical due to the enormous search space. Our proposed approach, Blind Image Restoration based on Kernel Mixture (BIRMK), improves upon this limitation by using a kernel function, specifically employing a Gaussian mixture as a kernel function, to model the image's pixel value distribution. By representing pixel value density as a kernel function, our approach allows for efficient computation of key images, which in turn enables effective degradation reversal even when the imaging parameters are unknown.

A recent concept, termed nonassociative Yang-Baxter equation, was introduced in 2019 as a dual framework for representation theory of bialgebras. This paper introduces a nonuniform equation equivalent to the relative R-matrix equation in this representation theory context. It was demonstrated that the nonuniform equation has practical applications in representation theory, particularly in constructing solutions to the relative R-matrix equation via direct sum and meromorphic gluing techniques. Moreover, a class of solutions to nonuniform equation was identified as cone cones, which possess a distinct geometric property under the dual action of a corolla. This section of the article showcases a method for constructing cones, initially developed in 2013 as a representation theory tool.

The correct operation of software significantly impacts real-world systems, with malfunctions leading to serious real-world consequences. The critical role that safety and reliability play in deployment drives software engineers to adopt formal validation methods like Hoare logic to ensure that safety requirements are met, often expressed using the framework of fractional differential equations. However, communicating these complex requirements to a broader audience is challenging, given a significant disparity between those who can contribute to software development and those capable of constructing logical statements. This disparity is exacerbated by the need for expertise in specialized formalisms to effectively communicate even basic safety information. This study proposes an innovative approach that harnesses the descriptive capabilities of everyday language to bridge this communication gap. By combining computational models, logic, and a transformer-based language model, we developed a system that automatically translates between software code and its associated descriptive language, enabling automated verification within the Hoare logic framework. Our experimental results demonstrate that our framework successfully validates safety and liveness properties, successfully validating 75% of assertions across various software programs, including 100% for a specific library, while also facilitating a novel form of automated reasoning that integrates machine learning capabilities.

Consensus algorithms are crucial for coordinating distributed systems, but they are highly sensitive to node failures, particularly in cases where nodes provide incorrect information. The RCanonical algorithm is a robust variant of Canopus, designed to withstand both node failures and the occurrence of Byzantine errors. By incorporating Byzantine-resilient data aggregation, RCanus maintains Canopus's performance characteristics while improving its overall robustness. Theoretical evaluations and real-world experiments demonstrate that RCanus outperforms Canopus in terms of robustness and exhibits comparable latency and throughput, even when no faulty nodes are present. Furthermore, simulations and experiments reveal that RCanus has a negligible overhead in processing additional checks when dealing with up to one faulty node, maintaining Canopus's efficiency.

To determine the bending modulus of lipid membranes containing cholesterol, 
we used an advanced molecular dynamics technique based on the undulating
membrane approach, which yielded results comparable to those obtained through
the traditional undulating plane method. We found that by using an 
optimized wave function based on a combination of two modes, we achieved a more
efficient and accurate estimation. We observed variations in the bending modulus
of the lipid assembly depending on cholesterol concentration. We found that the
clustering tendency of cholesterol increased the rigidity of the membrane in the
case of DOPC but had a negligible effect in the case of DPPC. We found that the
clustering threshold for cholesterol was around 20-25 mol%.

In this study, we investigate the quantum properties of the gravitational field using the Loop Quantum Gravity approach. By focusing on a simplified cosmological model known as the ADM Hamiltonian, we derive the quantum equations governing a spherical symmetric universe filled with a perfect fluid. Our analysis yields a set of canonical equations, which yield discrete eigenvalues for the gravitational field variables. These quantum equations reveal the quantum behavior of the gravitational field, providing insight into the quantum structure of the universe described by the ADM Hamiltonian model.

A comprehensive database is maintained by the Pierre Auger Observatory, cataloging all ultrahigh-energy cosmic ray and neutrino interactions that the observatory has detected during its initial 15 years of operation. During this period, the observatory collected an extensive amount of data on interactions, including 2691 events from the extensive air-shower surface detector and 163 triggered neutrino interactions. Notably, the observatory discovered 21 new highest-energy events exceeding 50 EeV and identified a record-breaking cosmic ray interaction at 6.18±0.42 (stat)±0.54 (syst) EeV. Overall, the catalog documents 242 new events surpassing 50 EeV energy threshold, contributing to our understanding of ultrahigh-energy cosmic ray phenomena.

In practical applications of object detection, understanding the uncertainty of predictions is crucial. This study introduces BayesOD, a Bayesian approach to evaluate the uncertainty of deep object detection models. It modifies object localization and classification tasks to align with Bayesian model averaging, incorporating probabilistic neural network outputs through a Monte Carlo sampling technique. Furthermore, this study develops an unsupervised reliability diagram refinement method, enhancing the accuracy of uncertainty assessments. Experiments were conducted on MS-COCO, demonstrating that BayesOD effectively correlates predicted uncertainty with actual error, outperforming alternative methods in both coverage and calibration aspects.

Predicting traffic patterns on specific routes is a critical task for many users.
Current studies primarily utilize large datasets from specific regions to forecast traffic conditions on given roads within that area.
However, these approaches are insufficient for users seeking accurate traffic predictions on unfamiliar roads lacking sufficient historical patterns.
To address this limitation, we propose a novel prediction method that considers traffic flowing patterns on any road within an unfamiliar environment.
This paper outlines a general framework for this problem, reviews relevant studies, and identifies specific challenges associated with this approach.

A key outcome shows that any given Gray category is equivalent to a category that is both fully coherent and coherent in nature. 
This significant result relies on a newly identified implementation structure, specifically the ability to implement the middle four rule within the context of n-categorial structures. 
This new implementation structure, specifically for the middle four rule, is shown to be a crucial component in the proof of the categorical nature of this result. 
The concept of implementation structures is a previously unexplored, but necessary tool in ω-categorial redefinition that is specifically relevant to the context of coherence.
