By training this module on a dataset of features extracted from a MobileNetV2 network, a convolutional neural network module is developed to predict whether a device is affected or not, using a Multi-Batch Label Attention (MLA) loss function. This design ensures robust performance even when the device's disturbance state changes over time. Experimental results on the CWA challenge benchmark demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance, achieving a Top-1 accuracy of 88.7% and a Top-3 accuracy of 94.9%, outperforming the baseline model by a margin of 2.2% and 4.9% respectively.

A novel spacetime configuration known as the Som-Raychaudhuri model describes a cosmic string that possesses both displacement and elasticity. Researchers have employed this spacetime configuration to study how charged particles under external forces behave in the context of the general relativistic framework. This study investigates how charged particles without external forces behave in the context of the general relativistic framework by employing the proper time along world lines as an equivalent to mass. This study involves the application of a novel technique for solving differential equations to obtain analytical solutions for the classical Klein-Gordon equation in the context of the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime configuration with a unique space-like displacement. By using this approach, researchers have established connections between energy and charge as well as energy and angular momentum. Furthermore, the study reveals that a gravitational field can influence a charged particle's motion, leading to associations between angular momentum and charge. By employing the Schrödinger equation in the context of the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime configuration with a unique space-like displacement, researchers have verified the validity of their findings from the general relativistic framework in the context of the Schrödinger equation.

Every measure algebra has a subgroup that behaves similarly to a measure algebra with the total measure restricted to the value 1, and is minimal in this context. In this study, we establish a condition for measure algebras that have the characteristic of being locally equivalent to the standard measure algebra $(\mathbb{T}, \lambda)$. Here, $\mathbb{T}$ is the unit circle and $\lambda$ represents the standard Lebesgue measure. Measure algebras sharing this property include a wide range of examples, such as the Haar measure algebra on a locally compact abelian group and the free measure algebra arising from an infinite abelian group, provided it has a countable generating set.

Our study focuses on the polarization of the proton in Deuteron via Compton scattering, focusing on the transverse skewness of the neutron within the Deuteron. By applying the final state interaction correction of the proton, our calculations reveal significant longitudinal and transverse spin asymmetries, emphasizing the necessity of incorporating FSI corrections when measuring these aspects experimentally. Moreover, we demonstrate that the polarization of the proton can serve as a valuable tool to distinguish between Generalized Parton Distributions and the Gerasimov-Drell-Hearn sum rule.

I suggest a new definition for Artificial Intelligence that goes beyond traditional computational systems and includes theoretical models of high intelligence. Artificial General Intelligence is defined as a versatile, efficient learning system capable of rapidly acquiring knowledge from limited data and applying it to solve various problems. The proposed framework integrates cutting-edge research from information theory, neural network learning, Bayesian statistics, and mathematics to inform the development of AGI systems. By combining theoretical models with practical applications, the framework offers novel approaches to AI problems and guides the construction of AGI systems through adaptive, iterative learning.

We've carried out theoretical research into the thermal shifts in the first sound velocity of the spin-orbit linked modulated superfluid as a function of temperature for correlated bosons in an optical lattice. We used the one-loop self-energy correction to the Higgs mode's self-energy within a self-consistent random phase approximation. We observed that the thermal shift in the first sound velocity initially decreases as the interaction strength increases up to a certain point and then starts to increase beyond that point, similar to the behavior of a self-energy correction's imaginary part. We also found that this thermal shift initially decreases as the hopping parameter decreases and then starts to increase after a certain point. We verified our findings using quantum Monte Carlo simulations and self-consistent quantum field theory-based quantum Monte Carlo transformations.

A class of graphs can be formed from finite abelian groups, with a potential application in achieving noiseless quantum queries. This study examines the limitations of graph coloring by a finite abelian group, specifically graph 色 deficiencies, and their implications for quantum queries. To address these limitations, the paper establishes a general criterion for a subset of finite abelian groups to give rise to graphs with minimal 色 deficiency, specifically -1 modulo the graph's chromatic number.  Further investigations reveal that graphs formed from the symmetric group S_n have a -1 modulo two chromatic number, while those from Q_n have a three modulo four chromatic number.  These findings suggest the possibility that quantum queries can resolve certain graph isomorphism problems, although certain problems remain unsolved.  The paper also defines a hierarchy based on graph 色 deficiency, establishing its equivalence with quantum query complexity and its correspondence with classical query complexity.  Finally, the hierarchy is illustrated with an example of graphs constructed from group operations, demonstrating a significant gap in quantum query complexity.

We have explored the relationship between N=4 super Yang-Mills theory and AdS_4/CFT, utilizing type IIA string theory. This was achieved through a rigorous analysis of BPS states in a novel, two-dimensional N=(4,4) supersymmetric spectrum, which resulted in the discovery of an exact spectrum of masses. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the compatibility of our results with previous studies involving the AdS_4/CFT correspondence. Our analysis also reveals the existence of a novel BPS spectrum, which we have computed the density of states for. Notably, our results have led to the identification of a precise value for the AdS radius, which we have shown to be in complete agreement with expectations.

Researchers are increasingly relying on Gaussian Process (GP) models for predictive tasks, yet there is often a lack of understanding behind the behavior of these models, primarily due to the arbitrary selection of kernels. This study focuses on developing GP kernels from basic mathematical functions, rather than through intuition or heuristics. By employing the techniques of differential geometry along with the assumptions of stationarity and isotropy, the authors derive a comprehensive set of kernels that can be utilized across various domains, including one-dimensional and two-sphere spaces. GP regressions on test datasets are performed using these newly developed kernels to showcase their performance. This novel approach may pave the way for developing kernels in other spaces, enabling the creation of Gaussian Process kernels for stations-geometries pairs in the future.

Beam-induced background, stemming from beam-beam effects, poses a significant challenge for high-luminosity muon colliders, necessitating precise monitoring and investigation. The majority of this beam-induced background is composed of beam-beam effects, which produce noise that hinders physics analyses by creating noise thresholds. The development of novel noise mitigation techniques is thus essential, with four key strategies identified: beam mitigation, beam noise manipulation, detector design and data analysis methods. The paper presents an overview of beam-induced noise, discusses specific beam manipulation methods and explores various noise mitigation tactics, with a focus on advanced muon colliders such as the International Muon Collider and the NCC.

We introduce a novel class of differentiable sparseness metrics,
regulated optimal transport (ROT), and show its equivalence to minimizing
weighted Hamming distance under specific conditions. ROT enables a variety
of supervised learning algorithms to utilize a wide range of Hamming-based
loss functions through optimal transport formulation. In addition, our
SparTen method effectively combines a task-specific loss with customized
sparseness metrics tailored for model compression. We demonstrate the
success of our approach on articulated pose estimation and object detection
in the wild, achieving significant reductions in model size with improved
results.

A unique behavior arises in certain systems of interacting bosons at low densities due to a process known as depletion, effectively preventing them from exhibiting the typical Bose-Einstein condensation beyond a specific point. This phenomenon is reminiscent of the Luttinger liquid theory, where it signifies a transition away from condensation, marking a transition between different phases of matter. In a model system consisting of Bose-Bose gases, researchers investigated this phenomenon by studying how the order parameter evolves as interactions weaken. They discovered a smooth transition characterized by a power-law relationship, specifically $c_1 \propto (1 - c_2 g)$, which indicates the boundary between two phases. This phenomenon can be understood in terms of a Luttinger parameter approaching infinity, effectively obstructing Bose-Einstein condensation. This behavior contrasts sharply with a more commonly observed first-order phase transition associated with Bose-Einstein condensation in gasses described by the Bogoliubov theory. The researchers confirmed these findings both numerically and experimentally, shedding new light on the interplay between weakly interacting bosonic systems and their behavior.

The concept of test odors was introduced to describe the noticeable negative effects that low-quality, unprofessional tests have on the well-being and productivity of software testers and developers. A notable characteristic of test odors is their contagious nature, spreading through a team and project over time. Despite their established existence in the field, the extent to which test odors impact a team remains unclear. A study involving 45 participants, comprising 21 software developers, was conducted to investigate the influence of test odors on developers as a group. The research revealed that developers perceive low-quality tests as inadequate tools, reducing their efficiency in performing their duties efficiently.

We develop a nonconvex differential equation, specifically a sweeping procedure for dynamic situations, which can be repurposed as a universal solver, effectively incorporating both convex and nonconvex perturbation-approach solvers for various problems of a nonconvex nature. Leveraging a newly created integrator for simulating nonconvex integro-differential equations, we illustrate its utility with a few specific uses.

The KKMCee software, a multi-photon Monte Event creator, is designed to produce Monte Carlo events for lepton and quark pair production at lepton colliders, allowing for precise generation of final state particles, including additional photons, in the process. Built as a multi-purpose tool, the program addresses various physical issues, employing state-of-the-art methods for initial state radiation calculation, beamstrahlung simulation, and beam polarization consideration. Furthermore, the software incorporates tools for final state radiation and particle decay, as well as for calculating cross sections. The KKMCee program addresses multiple issues arising from infrared divergences and collinear singularities, and compares its results to experimental data from the LEP, LHCb, and LHC to validate its accuracy.

Analyzing the timing between heartbeats can reveal critical information about an individual's cardiac health. This research introduces a novel technique for estimating the inter-beat interval using the Tiramizu framework. In approach, the Tiramisu framework's output is initially used to create a binary mask, which is then employed to extract unique features from ECG signals. It has been discovered that combining the previously separate features extracted using the Tiramisu framework leads to more effective outcomes. We validated our proposed method's efficacy through the TTM2 challenge, in which we achieved a mean absolute error of 3.3 milliseconds on test data, representing a 3.5 millisecond error reduction compared to year one's best performance. Furthermore, the novel approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques when tested on additional datasets.

Traditional randomization methods for low-rank tensor factorizations, such as those involving the tensor-T decomposition, typically limit the number of iterations to one, which can lead to suboptimal convergence in certain cases. To overcome this limitation, a new randomization technique has been developed that accommodates multiple iterations in tensor-T decomposition. Extensive experimentation on synthetic data demonstrates that increasing the number of passes can notably enhance convergence in tensor-T decomposition. Furthermore, a stochastic algorithm specifically designed for accelerating low-rank tensor-T decompositions is also proposed and shows improved efficiency over conventional methods through numerous trials.

Over the past decade, graph neural networks have demonstrated significant potential in solving real-world problems effectively. A primary limitation of these networks lies in their inability to capture the dynamic nature of real-world graphs. This paper delves into the various methods for representing graph nodes and edges in machine learning models, including traditional one-hot vectors and more sophisticated learned embeddings. These approaches aim to enhance the accuracy of graph neural networks in overcoming their static nature.

Our investigation focused on the very low-lying states of $^7$H and we calculated the electromagnetic form factors of the $^3$H+$4n$ resonance, where $4n$ is treated as four non-interacting neutrons. We analyzed these form factors in relation to those of elastic scattering and also computed their Coulomb and isospin scattering cross sections. These calculations can be verified through experiments involving $^7$H and $^3$H deep inelastic scattering.

This research tackles the Nirenberg issue for the conformal yellow equation on the half sphere, where there's no significant blow-up at the boundary's equator, a distinct difference from prior studies by Ambrozium - Baryer, non-trivial blow-ups at an interior point for the Nirenberg issue, and the half sphere, when there's no significant blow-up at the boundary's equator, we derive non-trivial blow-ups at an interior point for the Nirenberg issue, which is a notable difference from prior studies by non-trivial blow-ups at an interior point, we derive non-trivial blow-ups at an interior point, which is a notable difference from prior studies by deriving non-trivial blow-ups at an interior point, we derive non-trivial blow-ups at an interior point, which is a notable difference from prior studies.

Recent advancements in deep representation learning have led to innovative approaches leveraging convolutional neural networks and autoencoders, yet effective representation learning remains a challenge due to the difficulty in applying optimization techniques driven by specific tasks. This challenge can be addressed by leveraging unsupervised pretraining with density estimation, yet the standard maximum likelihood framework suffers from high computational costs, poor scalability, and suboptimal performance, as well as poor angles between data points in high-dimensional space. This limitation hinders efficient downstream task learning. This paper proposes two unsupervised learning algorithms, the first based on regularized Wasserstein depth and dynamic time warping, and the second on a data transformation approach converting input samples into weighted data clouds, leveraging Sinkhorn distances. This data transformation enhances representation learning capabilities, as evidenced by experimental results demonstrating improved performance in both generative and discriminative tasks across various datasets and network architectures.

In numerous countries, a strategy of decentralized testing and monitoring has been employed to curb the spread of COVID-19, with regional entities sharing data and implementing joint monitoring policies in England. This paper investigates the impact of regional cooperation on the regional monitoring efforts for COVID-19. We utilize mathematical modeling to simulate the local transmission dynamics of COVID-19, taking into account the effects of regional collaboration on monitoring efficacy in England. Our analysis reveals that regional cooperation has led to disparities in testing and contact tracing policies among different regions, resulting in varying capacities to detect and identify infected individuals. Consequently, some regions may not effectively utilize contact tracing due to insufficient regional detection rates, thereby undermining its potential benefits.

The cluster Melotte 72, a young and distant globular cluster located at 12.4 ± 0.8 kpc, was initially identified and studied by various astronomers, including Melotte, who discovered it in 1882. This study aims to characterize Melotte 72's position in the Galactic plane and analyze its member stars using the Gaia DR2 dataset, confirming it as a likely co-moving group rather than a true star cluster. By cross-referencing metal abundance data from spectroscopic observations, this work found a discrepancy between our determined distance and metal content and other studies. The findings indicate a distance of 12.4 ± 0.8 kpc and a metal content of [Fe/H] = -0.73 ± 0.02, suggesting a diverse star population with multiple subgroups.

We investigate the average number of Betti numbers for Gaussian polynomial maps $\mathcal{P}_d$ of a specified degree and dimension, with coefficients in a large but sparse interval $\mathcal{I}_N$ of size $N$, as $N$ approaches infinity. Our findings show that, for a map $\mathcal{P}_d$ with coefficients in this domain, its Kollar--Robertson indices, which serve as upper bounds for its topological invariants, are of a specific magnitude, specifically $N^{2(d+1)^{n-1}-1}$. This result is then used to derive an upper bound for the average number of Betti numbers as $N$ tends to infinity. To achieve this, we apply and extend certain algebraic and probabilistic principles in the context of polynomial rings.

The accuracy of camera intrinsics plays a vital role in computer vision tasks such as 3D reconstruction, object recognition, and pose detection. Inaccuracies stemming from manufacturing discrepancies, wear and tear, or environmental factors can significantly impact computer vision tasks. Although self-calibration techniques have been developed, they often require extensive data and time-consuming processing times, which can be impractical for real-world applications. This research presents an innovative method, which leverages the capabilities of deep learning to model camera adjustment from a single image, leveraging the knowledge encoded within a pre-trained convolutional neural network. Our approach involves fine-tuning the network to predict camera intrinsics, which demonstrates exceptional accuracy, achieving a notable reduction in root mean square error, specifically around 0.03, 0.005, and 0.01, respectively, in focal lengths and principal points. Furthermore, we investigate the efficacy of our method across various object types, encompassing spheres, cubes, and complex objects, showcasing its versatility and robustness.

A new inverse reinforcement learning method is proposed to determine an optimal policy from observed expert behavior, based on minimizing differences between the expected state visit frequencies following the expert policy and the desired policy. By focusing solely on learning a policy without learning a reward function, computational efficiency is prioritized. Through both synthetic and real-world experiments, the proposed approach demonstrates superior performance over existing methods.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission launched in 2013 with the goal of mapping the Milky Way galaxy in unprecedented detail. Its extensive dataset of over one billion stars offers a wealth of information to researchers studying galactic evolution. This article provides an overview of the mission's scientific objectives and highlights the anticipated breakthroughs that its data will enable.

For undirected graphs with treewidth at most $r$, finding a partition into at most three parts, such that removing any two parts leaves the remaining part connected, can typically be achieved with randomness in at most ${r\choose 2}$ steps. However, a long-standing problem remains in determining whether this number of phases can be determined deterministically within the same number of steps. We introduce two new, deterministic vertex-dividing algorithms for $r$-treewidth graphs, which operate within a specific time complexity and significantly reduce the required memory when $r$ is very large, achieving a memory complexity of $O(r^2\log^2 r)$. Specifically, one algorithm divides the graph into 3 parts with at most $r^2-r+1$ removals, while another division into 5 parts can be achieved with at most ${r\choose 2}+1$ removals, using a randomized process. These algorithms build upon previous work, including the use of random sampling, and provide valuable tools for creating tree decompositions locally with low memory usage.

The analysis of large networks with complex connections is a crucial challenge in social sciences, particularly for a subset of networks characterized by directional and induced relationships between categories. These networks, referred to as heterogeneous assessed networks, can reveal clustering patterns through the identification of communities within subgroups of these networks. However, due to computational limitations, methods to identify these communities in large, complex networks are limited. We introduce an innovative approach to identify induced communities within large, complex networks, focusing on their directional nature and incorporating weights to prevent artificially generated patterns. We demonstrate that our method accurately recovers hidden community patterns in simulated data, outperforming traditional block models. We also apply our approach to a real-world dataset, revealing previously unknown relationships within this dataset.

Traditional neural networks have been unable to effectively tackle complex problems due to their lack of embedded knowledge about the governing physics of the problem. To address this limitation, Physics-informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have been proposed as an alternative by incorporating equations into their training process. However, including these equations in their training process does not guarantee that the neural network will find the correct solution, especially when dealing with complex problems. To ensure that PINNs are used legally, we developed a new approach called authorized machine learning, which involves assessing the accuracy of the neural network after training based on specific criteria. To implement authorized machine learning, we employed an established mistake assessment method called the Hellinger distance, which measures the discrepancy between predicted and actual outcomes. By combining our authorized machine learning method with a previously developed local verification technique, we were able to develop a new neural network architecture that outperforms PINNs in solving complex heat transfer problems.

In epidemiological studies, understanding the impact of atmospheric contamination on disease transmission has gained increasing attention due to its relevance in non-infectious and infectious disease research. A significant hurdle in this area is the lack of suitable software for modeling and statistical analysis. To address this issue, this review explores the concept of air pollution and respiratory disease and introduces a model for atmospheric contamination that takes into account geographical and temporal factors. Various approaches to modeling contamination in epidemiological studies are examined, including geostatistical and artificial intelligence-based methods, and a comprehensive evaluation framework is provided. As an illustration, artificial intelligence methods are used to develop non-invasive models of PM2.5 and temperature across France, and the results are mapped.

To distinguish between the tunneling spectra of different types of bound states,  particularly Majorana modes and others like Andreev bound states or impurity states, is crucial. Recent theories suggest that the spectral features of tunneling modes can be distinguished not just based on their shapes but also through the electrical current they produce. In this technique, a normal metal electrode with a high resistance is used to create a weakly interacting system with a topological superconductor. The resulting tunneling spectra are highly dependent on the mixed conductance between the electrode and the superconductor. Unlike the case of a contact with negligible resistance, a weakly interacting system shows distinct characteristics, particularly near zero bias. By varying the electrode's resistance, one can control the shape of the tunneling spectrum and, consequently, identify tunneling peaks based on their unique responses to these changes in resistance. In a specific example involving a topological superconductor comprised of a ferromagnetic insulator and a topological insulator, our proposed method successfully differentiates Majorana modes from other types of bound states by analyzing how their tunneling spectra evolve with resistance and dissipative effects.

The study of linear bandits has garnered considerable interest in both academia and industry, driven by its capacity to tackle complex decision-making problems in diverse environments, often characterized by multiple domains. This disparity is compounded by the presence of varying subsets of actions across domains. Prior studies have addressed this challenge by assuming homogeneous action sets, but in reality, these subsets are often unique. Our study aims to tackle this gap by developing a Lineage-LB algorithm that accommodates diverse action sets, even when inferred from incomplete data. This approach enables the solution of complex decision-making problems in multi-domain settings, where tasks, such as network maintenance and product recommendation, inherently possess unique action subsets. Our findings demonstrate that the Lineage-LB algorithm achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(KT^2\sqrt{H})$, significantly lower than the $\tilde{O}(KT^3\sqrt{H})$ regret bound of a baseline algorithm, exemplifying the efficacy of our proposed approach.

Graphene exhibits exceptional electronic properties, particularly its Lande factor being nearly zero, which gives rise to a negligible valley Hall effect in place of a significant electronic Hall effect typically seen in other materials. However, a new phenomenon known as the Orbital Hall effect has been identified, which arises from a gradient in the lattice structure and has the potential to substitute the electronic Hall effect. To further enhance this phenomenon, a magnetic field can be applied perpendicularly to the graphene, which gives rise to a significant combined Hall effect known as the total Hall effect. Notably, a significant advantage of this new phenomenon is that it does not depend on a specific valley, allowing for a more accurate detection of the lattice's symmetry through valley sensitivity. Additionally, this new phenomenon exhibits a significant thermal stability, which could make it particularly useful for low-temperature applications in valleytronics.

The success of Graph Neural Network (GNN) on specific data sets is attributed to its ability to capture local graph patterns, but this capacity to learn from local environments also makes GNN vulnerable to adversarial attacks on graph data contamination tasks. To overcome this weakness, existing methods have attempted to improve GNN's performance by adjusting input graph structures or adding special sub-structures, however, their performance significantly degrades when facing novel adversarial attacks on different GNN models. This study proposes a reinforcement learning framework that learns optimal graph neural architectures capable of resisting adversarial attacks within a generative adversarial network framework. The learning process involves training two GNNs: the first one minimizes accuracy on a clean data set under adversarial attacks on structured graph contamination tasks, while the second maximizes AUC on the same data set under adversarial attacks, with these two networks competing against each other to generate contamination stategies. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods on various benchmark data sets.

To align astronomical catalogs, a common method involves matching objects based on their positions in the sky and their brightness, but the field of astrometry is currently advancing more rapidly than photometry. As a result, modern astrometric missions are capable of achieving precise position measurements for stars, but they often lack the multi-wavelength photometric data that is typically required for matching catalogs. In this study, we develop a novel approach to augment the limited photometric information available from single-wavelength astrometric data, allowing for more effective alignment of catalogs. Our method leverages the known properties of stellar atmospheres to predict the photometric bands for stars, which are then used to identify matching objects between different catalogs. We test the efficacy of our approach by augmenting the data from Gaia and matching it to the 2MASS and WISE catalogs, achieving improved alignment results compared to traditional methods.

We establish a minimal vertex subset $V'$ within an infinite graph or $k$-hypergraph, such that its structure remains unchanged when restricted to $V'$, under the appropriate topology defined by its original structure, if and only if the original structure belongs to specific localizations defined by finite sets and the complete structure is finite, in which case it localizes to itself. A key finding shows that a certain class of models does not satisfy the desirable properties in a certain context, specifically when considering certain first-order logic theories. Additionally, we establish continuous homogeneous models for certain structures, which are models that can be continuously transformed into each other, and which are either finite or can be viewed as specific topological spaces such as the Cantor space or a specific topological space associated with the first uncountable ordinal. Our work also introduces methods to obtain such models through product and quotient constructions.

Ontological knowledge graphs utilize hierarchical structures to establish precise definitions of concepts, setting boundaries and ensuring no overlapping definitions. However, in some instances, non-hierarchical relationships like symmetry are necessary. Existing visualization tools are often ineffective when dealing with large quantities of such data, particularly when concepts are distributed evenly across different hierarchical levels. OntoPlot addresses this challenge by introducing a visual representation that incorporates both hierarchical and non-hierarchical relationships, using a two-sided layout to accommodate notions like "every" and "implies". This innovative visualization approach is demonstrated through comparisons with established visualizations of the OWL BioPortal, revealing its capacity to enhance user comprehension of large knowledge graphs.

Automated speech recognition systems face challenges with domain shifts, which can cause performance degradation. This issue becomes more pronounced in end-to-end systems that combine speech audio and text processing into a single model. In this research, existing countercurrent domain adaptation techniques, specifically the CycleAD model, are extended to address this specific challenge, and several modifications are made to improve the cycleAD model for the end-to-end automated speech transcription systems. An additional entropy-based regularization method is applied to enhance the unsupervised speech recognition model's labeling accuracy, and the effectiveness of these approaches is evaluated on the Switchboard and LibriSpeech datasets within the end-to-end model framework. Experimental results demonstrate improvements in cross-domain speech recognition tasks, and a significant 6% relative error rate reduction is achieved on the LibriSpeech dataset when adapting from the TED-LS to the LibriSpeech domain.

To achieve fully autonomous agent navigation, researchers have employed active deduction as a method for tackling tasks that demand goal-oriented decision-making. Building upon this, the proposed self-governing navigation framework integrates active deduction with vision, control, and learning to enable agents to accomplish diverse objectives in disparate environments. The core framework consists of a top-down planner that leverages active deduction to devise a sequence of actions for robots to attain their objectives. These actions are generated within an abstract state space representation tailored to each robot's objective. For tasks unachievable through pre-programmed action sequences, the robot employs vision-based feedback to identify suitable actions in real-world settings. Additionally, the system utilizes machine-learned control to improve navigation precision and adapt to vision-based feedback. As a result of this research, the robot demonstrates the capacity to accomplish multiple new objectives without necessitating re-planning, and it can also acquire control policies for pre-planned action sequences to enhance navigation accuracy.

We introduce a novel theoretical model to explain why soft spheres exhibit a higher density on the cold side of a thermal gradient compared to hard spheres. By analyzing polymeric liquids and surfactant solutions, an entropic model suggests that the disordered configurations of soft molecules create additional volume, which becomes concentrated in the cold side through convective transport under a thermal gradient.

Recent advancements in automated music composition have seen significant improvement, 
with contemporary transformer-based models leading the way in creating original pieces. 
However, accurately evaluating the quality of compositions from these models remains a 
challenging issue. In this research, we examine how different neural networks can serve as 
evaluation metrics for automated music composition, testing their effectiveness in identifying 
compositions that align with how humans perceive music quality. We also develop a new method 
for evaluating model-generated music that combines multiple effective neural networks and find that 
this approach leads to more accurate results that correlate with how humans judge music quality.

Adaptation techniques have been widely applied in human identification tasks to address issues such as domain shift and data scarcity. In particular, deep feature alignment methods have shown potential in this area. Nonetheless, these techniques often produce similar features for the same individual across various cameras, resulting in a large number of redundant predictions. In this research, we introduce an innovative post-classification reordering approach for adaptive pedestrian identification tasks. Our proposed method efficiently reduces the number of false positives in unsupervised domain adaptation settings by leveraging the inherent spatial locality of human appearance. Experimental results on widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing the performance of state-of-the-art unsupervised domain adaptation methods with minimal computational overhead.

The field of music processing has garnered significant attention due to its
potential in creating personalized music experiences.  Various applications
include adaptive music for games and interactive sound systems, but the
upcoming generations of gaming systems and virtual reality technologies
will further amplify the requirements for generating immersive soundscapes.
In line with these advancements, this paper proposes a novel approach to
transform musical audio into spatially captured sound, enabling vocoding-based
audio recovery.  This process is analogous to non-semantic image translation,
yet the goal is to preserve the original musical structure while facilitating
spatial reconstruction.  Our proposed method combinesvocoding-based audio
transformation with a spatial reconstruction technique, resulting in an
enhanced audio quality that outperforms the limitations of conventional music
processing techniques.

The impetus behind throwing actions is to send an object on a desired path to a specific location. Research has primarily centered on the throw's beginning phase, with little attention given to the point of release, despite its critical role. This research investigates how releasing an object prematurely or post-optimally affects accuracy and efficiency during throwing movements. A throwing simulation and accompanying dataset were developed to examine these nuances and assess whether executing a perfect throw from a suboptimal release point yields the same outcome as a flawed throw with a precise release point. The findings suggest that premature release compromises both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, it was discovered that executing a perfect throw from a suboptimal release point can produce a more stable movement than a flawed throw with a precise release point, with implications for robotic and human throwing performance.

We introduce a novel neural machine translation (NMT) decoding method called formed decoding, which enhances sentence parsing and understanding during generation by introducing a tree structure that represents the sentence's syntax. Formed decoding initiates parsing from an empty tree and gradually incorporates links one at a time, ensuring that the final sentence's parsing aligns with its optimal structure based on joint probability. This approach's parameters can be learned through maximum likelihood estimation. Notably, formed decoding not only facilitates the acquisition of better alignments between words and phrases but also enables the integration of syntactic information into generated sentences. Additionally, it offers a straightforward mechanism for incorporating hard syntactic constraints into NMT, thereby streamlining the process of inducing sentence parsing during NMT model training. Experimental results on the WMT 2017 and 2018 English-to-German datasets demonstrate that formed decoding enhances sentence parsing accuracy and improves translation quality.

Interstellar dust formation is a challenging process that involves the formation of larger molecules through stepwise additions of single atoms and ions to seed particles, driven by surface reactions. Researchers rely heavily on spectroscopic data and laboratory experiments to determine the binding energies of these species, which are crucial for modeling dust formation in interstellar space. A new open-access database has been developed to provide accurate binding energy data for astrochemically significant species interacting with common dust components, giving researchers a vast resource of over 100,000 binding energy values derived from over 1,000 quantum chemical calculations. This database, known as Binding Energy Assessment Platform, serves as an essential resource for dust formation research and dust-related surface reactions in astrophysics and astrochemistry.

This study focuses on the multiplicative stochastic model with a sample-related lower limit for positive random variables and its estimation of unknown scale and shape parameters using a log-transformed multiplicative error model. To achieve this, the evaluation encompasses estimation methods including unbiased, least squares, and maximum likelihood estimators for scale, as well as two different minimum variance estimators for shape, resulting in calculated variances and covariance of the estimators. The computational efficiency of the estimators is examined through simulation, utilizing specific probability distributions such as lognormal, gamma, uniform, and power law distributions.

A novel approach called shallow shades is presented for efficiently evaluating the depth properties of arbitrary single-qubit Clifford unitaries through random circuits. By using low-depth circuits and mid-circuit measurements, these unitaries can be prepared with higher all-success probabilities compared to existing methods. This leads to faster convergence when estimating circuits with higher probabilities, and enables faster collection of data, especially for circuits with probabilities greater than 0.5. By integrating shallow shades with existing techniques, we can prepare single-qubit Clifford circuits with 99% all-success probability using just 10 circuits, compared to 20 circuits with traditional approaches. This represents a 50% reduction in the number of circuits needed. Additionally, we can estimate the leading term's coefficient of circuits with 50% probability with an accuracy of 1% after measuring a mere 1000 samples for circuits with probabilities exceeding 0.5. Moreover, we can approximate circuits with probabilities up to 99.9999993% after collecting 1000 samples. Furthermore, shallow shades is compatible with mid-circuit correction, allowing us to estimate circuits with probabilities up to 99.9999993% after collecting data from 10 circuits. Finally, we demonstrate that shallow shades can accurately evaluate random Clifford circuits and their corresponding CNOT circuits with up to 50 qubits.

The reflection coefficient's significant $|k|$ behavior for the Davey-Stewartson II equations has been established, particularly for the Cauchy problem in the half-plane. This research covers two scenarios: one where the surface data is in $H^{s,0,0}$ with $s>3/2$, and another where $s\in(1,3/2]$. For smaller values of $s$, reflection coefficients are defined on the negative half-plane.

This research focuses on faking resilient machine learning models that function well on adversarially altered inputs. The work expands existing adversarial robustness methods like adversarial training, adversarial debiasing, and adversarial Adversarial-Aware Regularization to handle scenarios where some training data inputs are maliciously generated. These scenarios are called Sibyl, named after a Byzantine figure, to describe machines learning from data with maliciously generated examples. Adversarial training is found ineffective in high Sibyl frequencies, whereas adversival debiasing and adaversarial regularization show robust performance at Sibyl frequencies of up to 50-60%. We explore how frequency thresholds vary across different tasks and data sets.

A new meta-learning method called Meta-Learning Depictions (MetaLD) is proposed to automatically learn how to represent objects and their arrangements in a consistent visual language, enabling both demonstration of unfamiliar configurations and adaptation to new environments. By representing the object's arrangement as a linear depiction, meta-adaptation is facilitated through a module-based design that simplifies learning about unfamiliar objects and their arrangements. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MetaLD in learning how to depict linear arrangements on a Lego system, and show that it can handle objects of various shapes, colors, and arrangements, even in complex 2D scenarios.

High-performing multilingual language models from organizations like Facebook and Google have greatly enhanced state-of-the-art machine translation capabilities for various languages. However, their resource requirements are immense, making deployment on devices with limited resources impractical. To overcome this challenge, researchers have turned to model compression techniques such as quantization and knowledge distillation to efficiently utilize computational resources while maintaining high performance levels. Yet, their effectiveness has been questioned due to the sensitivity of these techniques to hardware variations. This study investigates how robust quants and distilled models are to hardware prunes, revealing that they are generally brittle in this context. To counter this issue, the research explores whether ensembling multiple model architectures can enhance the robustness of quants and distilled models, while also demonstrating the benefits of quants ensembles over both existing quants and distilled models on a set of benchmark languages, without sacrificing a considerable amount of accuracy.

In recent years, the study of $k$-Lagrange function has garnered significant interest within mathematical research. This function's research involves analyzing maximum weight sum scenarios under diverse constraints within a given structure called a hypergraph, specifically focusing on its solitary form. The study of solitary $k$-Lagrange function has led to notable outcomes, particularly in identifying relationships with well-known mathematical conjectures such as Ramsey theory and Turán problems. Building upon existing research, this study delves into solitary $k$-Lagrange functions by introducing a newly defined hypergraph known as $\Lambda_{k,n}$ and examining its solitary $k$-Lagrange function properties. Specifically, this research examines the behavior of the Lagrange function as it relates to its dual graph's edge sum and path complexity. Notably, the study achieves its primary objective by determining the asymptotic behavior of the Lagrange function for large values of the variable $n$.

In recent years, deep learning techniques have garnered significant attention in the medical image segmentation field. However, these methods typically necessitate substantial amounts of annotated data and fail to account for variations in imaging conditions. To address these challenges, we have developed an innovative two-stage framework that leverages unsupervised image enhancement and pneumonia detection. The unsupervised image enhancement module generates high-quality synthetic images, and a change detection module identifies enhancements associated with high detection rates. A stage-adaptive loss function, incorporating a mix of supervised and unsupervised losses, further optimizes change detection performance. Moreover, our change enhancement module can effectively transfer pneumonia segmentation knowledge from synthetic images to real images, allowing for accurate segmentation even with limited data. We tested our method using three datasets, demonstrating substantial improvements in performance, specifically an 11.1% increase on the public LiTS dataset, accurate predictions on the ChaFI dataset, and notable advancements with small datasets, showcasing reduced data requirements.

To effectively utilize AI systems, particularly those based on AI, it's crucial for users to provide precise and detailed instructions, known as prompts. However, users' natural language descriptions can be ambiguous, leading to difficulties in conveying their intended meaning clearly. This paper addresses the issue by proposing a versatile system called MPrompt, which processes and refines user inputs to create adaptable prompts. By utilizing a language model to extract key information and a categorization system to organize these into information types, MPrompt restructures the input. It then employs a state-of-the-art language model to rephrase the collected information into prompts tailored to specific AI models from OpenAI and Google. By testing MPPrompt on multiple AI-generated content models, our research demonstrates its ability to significantly boost instruction-following accuracy, up to 30% in some cases, by optimizing prompts that yield more accurate generated responses.

This paper explores the 'causal effect' of a treatment effect's impact on an explanatory factor (S) and an outcome (Y), with the 'causal effect of a damage' referring to instances where the former shows no variation but the outcome varies significantly. To investigate this, the study employs Smith-Vanderbyl's (2008) do-calculus framework, revealing specific requirements for identifying the causal effect of damage. Furthermore, it presents a case study illustrating the application of Smith-Vanderbyl's definition in the context of physical damage.

This study introduces a deep learning framework specifically designed for educational purposes.  By leveraging the MMLSpark library and Spark Cluster capabilities, this framework offers versatility in both flexibility and scalability.  Its various features and capabilities are thoroughly examined, and benchmarks are set to compare performance with state-of-the-art deep learning frameworks and libraries.

A speech system's voice changer aims to transform an input voice into a desired target voice, achieving voice re-synthesis without the necessity of a speech dataset sampled from both voices. This research presents Zero-shot Voice Change, a zero-shot approach to voice changing. Specifically, this study introduces two previously unexplored re-synthesis methods: a zero-shot extension of voice conversion and a transfer learning-based model of voice synthesizer. Experimental results indicate that the proposed Zero-shot Voice Change effectively addresses voice changing tasks.

We establish existence and uniqueness principles for solutions to systems governed by the generalized Coleman-Gurtin equation, incorporating a boundary condition driven by a stochastic process and set within a bounded domain in n-dimensional space with n equal to 1, 2, or 3. We demonstrate that our findings encompass systems akin to the Coleman-Gurtin and Perzyna plasticity model with a similar boundary condition driven by stochasticity.

To address the growing uncertainty in daily electricity consumption caused by widespread adoption of smart home technologies, researchers have developed a new method for forecasting low-voltage grid load. This probabilistic forecast combines daily maximum and minimum single-home consumption with corresponding time-window probabilities. Extensive data from over 50,000 consumers was used to develop this forecast, confirming that low-voltage grid load largely follows a daily double-Pareto distribution. To achieve accurate probabilistic predictions, an ensemble model was created by combining multiple machine learning algorithms, with Random Forests achieving the best results. This approach not only outperformed other individual models but also provided reliable probabilistic forecasts for a wide range of scenarios, including forecasting daily highs.

The increasing popularity of AI technology has led to numerous AI models being developed across various fields. However, domain-specific knowledge integration remains a significant challenge, despite the potential benefits of expert systems and knowledge graphs in facilitating expert knowledge contribution. This paper presents a systematic approach to incorporating domain expertise into machine learning models, drawing on insights from literature reviews and use-case analysis. By doing so, this study aims to guide future research in natural language processing and beyond. Ultimately, this paper seeks to answer the question of how domain expertise can be effectively incorporated into AI models.

Current image segmentation techniques rely heavily on the knowledge of specific class locations, limiting their applicability to experiments with predefined constraints. This paper addresses Dynamic U-Net (DU-Net), an extension of U-Net that eliminates the need for class location information by utilizing weakly labeled datasets. DU-Net's architecture was designed based on prior research into knowledge transfer and can be effectively trained using only weakly labeled images. The model's performance was evaluated using the second version of the COVID-19 Dataset for Localization and Segmentation (COVID-LS2) and compared with other state-of-the-art models. The results indicate that these models have typically been trained with fully supervised methods and further analysis was conducted on how the availability of ground truth boundaries affects both fully and weakly supervised approaches. The study concludes that DU-Net achieves satisfactory and competitive results under specific conditions, and that it performs well in both dynamic and static topologies.

A significant challenge in clinical practice and research is automating the identification of vertebrae through volumetric imaging. This study introduces a new technique, based on deep learning, for automatically locating and marking vertebrae in CT scans, particularly of the lumbar spine. We first develop a 3D deep learning approach that rectifies the lumbar spine in 3D, thereby rectifying the irregular and curved nature of the spine. We then transform the problem of identifying vertebrae into one of segmenting the spine in two dimensions. We leverage a deep learning model that segments the spine in three dimensions and utilizes transfer learning to generate two-dimensional images that conform to anatomical relationships. We further refine the generated vertebrae by applying anatomically-informed rules. We evaluate our method on public datasets, specifically the public and private lumbar spine datasets, and assess its performance against existing methods. Our experimental results show that our method outperforms existing methods in both public and private datasets, with an average improvement of 10.6% and 8.2%, respectively. We also demonstrate the efficacy of our method in automating vertebrae localization and recognition tasks through experimental evaluation.

Our research focuses on the resonant scattering of a single electron by a highly excited photon trapped within a cavity, a scenario characterized by extremely strong interaction. Utilizing second quantization, we establish a four-level model to simulate this unique electron-photon coupling. We observe that under conditions of dynamical stabilization, where vacuum oscillations are suppressed, the probability of electron-photon scattering is significantly reduced, yielding a "transmission window." Furthermore, we demonstrate that in dynamical stabilization, the photon's polarization is flipped from circular to linear, a phenomenon attributed to the influence of a vacuum-related term in the modified Hamiltonian, a consequence of strong interaction. Lastly, we establish a connection between dynamical stabilization, a shifted electron energy level caused by strong interaction, and a previously reported phenomenon where vacuum inhibition leads to a redshift of photon energy.

A key goal in quadruped locomotion involves leveraging the resilience in limbs to mitigate the impact of disturbances. Although conventional stiff-legged designs excel at handling minor disruptions through passive damping, this capacity diminishes as the disturbance's magnitude increases. In contrast, actuators incorporating built-in elasticity have been shown to expand the quadrant of stability and improve post-fall recovery, albeit at a cost of decreased performance when handling small disturbances. In this paper, we demonstrate that integrating the advantages of both approaches – elastic leg passivity and active control – through a unified framework powered by elastic actuators and feasible via our elastic actuated quadruped. We employ a soft-body-inclusive whole-body controller paired with a soft-body fall correction module, trained through reinforcement learning in a precise, physics-based environment, to successfully adapt the controller's performance to both small and large disturbances. Experimental outcomes, encompassing both controlled and uncontrolled disturbances up to 10kg, reveal that the proposed active control system surpasses passive counterparts in the efficacy of its small disturbance mitigation by a factor of 1.8, ultimately culminating in the quadruped's enhanced overall robustness against all-sized disturbances.

This study proposes a quantum analogue of the Euler-Lagrange differential equation, defining $n$-th order quantum Lagrangians for non-commutative variables $\phi_a$ as functions of $\phi_a$, $\phi_{a, \mu_1}$, $\phi_{\mu_1, \mu_2}$,... $\phi_{\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3}$. We define a quantum $\partial_\mu$ operator as $\phi_{\mu} = \Delta \partial_{\mu} \phi$, where $\Delta$ is a deformation parameter. This equation is used to construct the quantum $n$-th order Euler-Lagrange equation, and this equation is used to determine conditions under which a quantum field $\phi_a$ is $\kappa$-quotientable for positive integers $\kappa$. This study also discusses the relationship between the quantum Euler-Lagrange equation and the Weyl-Moyal algebra.

A compact, 30 cm diameter plasma device featuring a linear magnetic field configuration has been utilized to investigate the tearing instability in the collisionless regime. This unique experimental setup enables the thorough investigation of fundamental magnetic reconnection processes at a laboratory scale. During the instability development, an isolated magnetic island forms, which initially exhibits slow growth due to unstable electron dynamics caused by the island's curvature effects. As the tearing mode progresses, the island experiences rapid growth, indicating the emergence of kinetic electron dynamics that effectively drive magnetic reconnection. These experimental observations align with theoretical predictions and collisionless plasma simulations initially reported by H. Plump et al., Phys. Plasmas 22, 052102 (2015).

Fashion image retrieval using raw pixels is a complex task.  The challenge is
due to variations caused by factors such as pose, lighting, and camera angle,
as well as manipulations like cropping, blurring, and filters, all of which affect
the fashion attributes being searched for. To address this issue, we introduce
a method that extracts and incorporates high-level, semi-supervised features
into fashion attribute-based retrieval systems. Our technique consists of two
components: a feature extractor trained with a loss function designed to minimize
mismatches caused by non-manipulation factors, and a feature manipulator that
mitigates the effects of image manipulations. When evaluating our method on
attribute-based retrieval, it significantly outperforms existing approaches both
visually and numerically.

The task of dual gradient ascent is to develop algorithms that can effectively address a class of challenging problems, including both convex optimization and inverse problems, in a more general setting of Banach spaces, beyond the limitations of Euclidean spaces. These problems are particularly challenging due to their inherent ill-posedness, necessitating the use of specialized regularization techniques. We demonstrate the efficacy of dual gradient ascent methods in solving these problems, leveraging dual norms for step size calculations and convexity in a combination with Tychonoff regularization for development of proposed algorithms. The theoretical foundation of dual gradient ascent is built upon duality theory in Banach spaces, enabling its application to a diverse range of optimization and inverse problem problems.

Assessing depth maps created from light field data is crucial for further data processing, but current evaluation metrics are hindered due to corresponding image mismatches. The standard metric for this assessment is the OCRE, but it fails in areas with occlusions, resulting in inaccurate visual assessments. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel OCRE variant, called OCREC. The OCREC technique reevaluates the target depth value by taking into account the response from reference depth maps when they are partially obscured by occlusions - essentially, it considers depth value contributions from occluded regions to determine the most suitable target depth value. Experimental outcomes on two distinct datasets demonstrate the superiority of OCREC over conventional metrics in both qualitative and quantitative terms. Furthermore, the proposed metric is available for public use on our GitHub platform.
The approach utilizing the bilinear method to derive the Fokas-Lenells equation, along with its associated spectral problem, is presented in this investigation.

Our research centers on the Atiyah-Singer index theorem, which facilitates conversion between dual formulations in field theory. By extending this principle, we can derive non-Riemannian gravitational actions from their duals in the Sp(4,R) supergravity theory. However, this extension isn't as straightforward as in the N=0 case, necessitating careful consideration of how action and equations of motion transform. Consequently, we observe that some gravitational actions only have duals in the path integral framework, while others are present in both the path integral and stationary phase approximations.

In order to optimize the effectiveness of wireless in-home WiFi networks, we have developed a method for automatically selecting access points and extenders based on channel load information. Our solution involves a novel type of wireless measurement called the "channel load measurement action frame," which allows clients to assess the current channel congestion of an AP or extender. By utilizing this information, clients can efficiently locate the most suitable AP or extender for connection. Our approach is rooted in the extended IEEE 802.11v standard framework, providing a reliable mechanism for managing wireless roaming and improving overall network performance.
